item.title: Global warming beyond Paris Agreement targets is now a given, UN says. Experts say it should be a call to action, not apathy.
item.description:
Under the Paris Agreement, countries pledged to make an effort to limit global warming to 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, in order to avoid intense impacts of climate change.

But that level of warming is now “widely assessed as unavoidable,” according to a new report from the United Nations Environment Programme titled “Limiting Overshoot.” 

Our planet is likely to surpass 1.5°C within the next few years. 

The best case scenario—if all national climate plans are fully implemented and net-zero targets reached—is now a world with 1.8°C of warming.

Many countries are not on that path, however. As of 2025, only 15 countries even met the Paris Agreement’s deadline for submitting their plans to cut greenhouse gas emissions.

More likely is a world with 2.6°C of warming, which the UN says we could hit by 2100 under current policies. 

Still, climate experts warn people not to give up on climate actions. Though that reality may seem discouraging, there are still meaningful steps we can take, they say, to avoid “cascading climate impacts.” 

And every action matters: though we’ll likely see intense climate impacts, “every fraction of a degree avoided…will save lives, protect ecosystems and reduce economic losses,” per the report.

A 1.5°C world is inevitable—but it isn’t safe

Though we’ve made some global progress to address climate change, these efforts haven’t cut greenhouse gas emissions quickly enough to avoid that 1.5C threshold, per the UNEP report.

That doesn’t mean a world with more than 1.5°C of warming is “safe or acceptable,” it adds: “There are no benign scenarios with global temperature rise above this level.”

Such warming comes with faster sea-level rise; a higher likelihood that ecosystems like coral reefs will collapse; more wildfires and extreme heat; and drastic loss of ice sheets, glaciers, permafrost, and snow. 

“While there are uncertainties around the timings and strength of these impacts and tipping points, it is clear they will harm people, societies and economies,” the report reads. 

All those impacts will threaten food security and global water supplies; they also raise the risk of deadly pathogens.

Because our emissions reductions haven’t occurred fast enough, pathways to reduced warming that were once available around the time of the Paris Agreement are “no longer feasible.” We would have needed to enact “immediate, deep, and sustained” reductions in greenhouse gas emissions as early as 2015 or 2020.

We need net-negative emissions

Surpassing that 1.5°C threshold is now, essentially, a given.

The global goal is no longer to limit warming in that way, but to get on a pathway of “overshoot, peak and decline,” the UN says—meaning that we keep that warming to the lowest possible level and then bring it down by the end of the century, while implementing climate change adaptation efforts.

Instead of aiming for net-zero emissions, countries will now need to work towards being “net-negative,” via carbon dioxide removal, in order to reverse global warming. 

Cutting our greenhouse gas emissions in the first place is still crucial; we can’t emit the same amount of pollution and only rely on carbon capture. Every year of high emissions makes limiting our global warming more difficult, the report says.

And our emissions do remain at record highs: In 2024 alone, fossil fuels and industry produced around 40 gigatons of CO2 (one gigaton is about one billion metric tons). 

If we keep that pace, we’ll surpass 1.5°C in just about three years. 

We can’t let UN report be a ‘call to apathy’

Along with carbon removal, the UN report emphasizes the need for “transformational adaptation” to protect people and ecosystems from climate change’s impacts. 

But the report’s focus on this is concerning to other climate experts. 

“Transformational adaptation is distinct from the urgent and growing need to address present and future losses and damages, said Rosanne Martyr of Climate Analytics, a Berlin-headquartered science and policy institute, in a statement. 

Climate Analytics worries that the UN report could be a “call to apathy, not to arms.” 

“Although UNEP does a good job of describing the hole we’ve dug ourselves into, it does a poor job of showing us that there is a way out,” Bill Hare, Climate Analytics CEO and a former lead author on Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change assessments, said in a statement. 

Though the UNEP report talks about the need to reduce emissions, and frequently notes the role of fossil fuels to produce such emissions, it makes just one mention of the need for a “fossil fuel phase-out.”

“Structural shifts are slow and institutionally and politically challenging,” the report reads, “reinforcing the need to anticipate net-negative targets and avoid fossil fuel lock-in through near-complete phase-out.” 

And while the UNEP report says that we must “hold fast to global commitments under the Paris Agreement,” it doesn’t overtly remind governments of their responsibility to deliver on such commitments, Climate Analytics says. 

It’s governments’ “repeated failure,” per Climate Analytics, that has made surpassing 1.5C of warming “inevitable.”

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: US envoy to visit Kyiv in coming days, Zelenskyy says, as Putin signals ‘chance’ of peace
item.description:
Negotiators to visit Kyiv and Moscow as US president Donald Trump says he wants to see an end to the war. What we know on day 1,654

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that US negotiators will ⁠soon visit Moscow and ⁠Kyiv to resume efforts to end the Russian invasion. The Ukrainian president said in his nightly video address that preliminary dates had been set for the visit. “We expect to see representatives of the US president here in Kyiv,” Zelenskyy said. “There will be a meeting with them in Moscow and in Kyiv. We are ​expecting a meeting with them in the coming days. It is very ‌important. It is important that America continues ‌to be active.”

Meanwhile, Vladimir Putin said on Thursday there was a chance of reaching an agreement to end the war in Ukraine. Speaking at an economic ​forum, Russia’s president said a number of countries including the US and China were ready to support a peace settlement. “Ultimately, however, the problem must be resolved by the countries involved in the conflict – Russia ⁠and Ukraine,” he said. “We are grateful to everyone attempting to contribute to a settlement. Is there a chance? In my view, yes, there is.”

In Washington, Donald Trump said he wanted to see an end to the war and losses sustained by both sides. “I just want ‌to see that end. I think we’ll get it,” the US president told GB News in an interview that aired on Thursday, a day after telling reporters he wanted a summit with Putin when the Kremlin leader is ready for a peace deal. They last met for US-mediated talks in February.

Trump has said he would ask ⁠European nations to pay back the US for military aid and munitions previously sent to Ukraine amid the ongoing war with ⁠Russia and appeared to signal ⁠a halt ​in sales to allied nations. In a social media post, Trump on Thursday also slammed reports of heavily depleted US munition stockpiles amid the ⁠separate war in Iran, while adding that the US was ramping up production and stockpiling munitions. “We are taking them for ourselves, the U.S.A., ⁠rather than selling them to others, but the sales to Allies will soon again, begin,” Trump ​wrote.

A Ukrainian strike ⁠on Thursday killed four people, ⁠including two ⁠medical ​personnel, in an attack ⁠on Russia’s border region of Belgorod, officials ⁠said. The region’s official ​headquarters said the ‌dead in Shebekino, just across the border from Ukraine, included a doctor, ‌medic and married couple. ​Three people were injured. Meanwhile, the head of Russian-controlled parts of ⁠eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk Region said ​three ​civilians died in ​drone strikes ‌in ​three ​separate districts of the region.

Russian drones struck and damaged a Coca-Cola ⁠plant outside the Ukrainian capital Kyiv on Thursday, Zelenskyy said. Officials ⁠said ​there were no injuries in the strike near the town ⁠of Brovary, east of the capital. “Today, the Russians have hit ⁠a Coca-Cola plant with their drone. Coca-Cola ​is such ‌an enemy that ‌they set it on fire ‌with their Shaheds,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address, referring to Iranian-designed drones. “It’s a clear Russian signal to America. The Russians cannot be unaware that ‌this is an American facility.”

A Russian attack on ⁠the Ukrainian capital Kyiv ⁠on ​Thursday injured 10 people, triggered a fire and badly damaged a high-rise ⁠residential building, officials said. The city’s military administration initially said one person had died ⁠in the latest assault, but later said ​the report had proved ‌untrue. It said 10 ‌people, including a child, had been hurt. The capital’s mayor, Vitali ‌Klitschko, said nine people were injured, including six medical personnel.

item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy links Russian strikes on Kyiv airports to US envoys’ visit
item.description:
Moscow attacked Kyiv and Boryspil international airports as talks yielded no evident change in Vladimir Putin’s peace demands. What we know on day 1,656

Russian attacks on Kyiv and Boryspil international airports were “clearly” a reaction to the possibility of the US negotiators flying to Kyiv after talks in Moscow, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has said. On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had “taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky. Of course, there are and will be no threats to diplomacy from our side.” Both airports service the Ukrainian capital.

There was no comment from the US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who were visiting Moscow for the first time since January. They flew out of Moscow soon after the talks and were ‌due to meet Zelenskyy in Kyiv ‌on Sunday. The Kremlin’s tone appeared unchanged. After three hours of talks, an aide to Vladimir Putin, Yuri Ushakov, said the Russian president had told the US pair that Russia was making “real progress” on the battlefield, was confident of achieving ⁠its goals, and stressed the necessity of addressing “all the root causes of the conflict”. Ushakov said ​the Americans had “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement”, but he did not say what those ideas were.

The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250km (775-mile) frontline. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv. Kremlin spokesperson ‌Dmitry Peskov posted online that Putin had ordered the military not to strike Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight on Saturday. However, he said Russia had not yet agreed to a broader three-day ceasefire. Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow through to Monday.

Russian attacks killed five employees and wounded five others at an industrial facility in the Dnipropetrovsk region, said the local military administration head, Oleksandr Hanzha. “A locksmith, an electrician, a plumber and a machinist. People of peaceful professions. They were simply working their shift. They were doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives.” Russia’s defence ministry said it had carried out strikes on two metallurgical plants that it claimed were sites for military production.

A 62-year-old man was wounded, and several homes and an apartment building damaged, in a separate attack on the region’s Nikopol district, Hanzha said. The city of Dnipro and the nearby Pidhorodne community were among the areas hit. One person died and five other were injured, including two men who were hospitalised in serious condition. A sixth civilian was injured in an attack on the Nikopol district.

Other deadly Russian attacks took place in Chuhuiv in Ukraine’s eastern Kharkiv region, on the Bucha district of Ukraine’s Kyiv region, and on a shopping centre in the southern Mykolaiv region. In Russia’s Belrogod region on the border with Ukraine, two people were killed and three others wounded by Ukrainian attacks on Saturday, local authorities said. Russia launched ballistic missiles from its Rostov and Voronezh regions and deployed 167 attack drones, Ukraine’s air force said on Saturday.

item.title: Gas prices break Labor Day weekend records as Iran War and refinery issues continue
item.description:
It’s never been more expensive in the U.S. to fill up the tank and take one last summer trip over the Labor Day weekend.

The average price of regular gas was $4.14 a gallon heading into the holiday, nearly a dollar higher than last year and well above the Labor Day weekend record of $3.82 from 2012, according to AAA motor club.

Nicole Collins planned to head from Philadelphia to South Carolina to visit friends, but she said her family has spent most of the summer close to home and not taking their typical weekend trips because driving has gotten so expensive.

“Gas is pretty high right now. It doesn’t help that we also have a baby, so we also have to pay for that,” Collins said outside a gas station in Claymont, Delaware, where regular gas was $4.199 a gallon.

Prices shot up after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in February and have not settled down since. Crude oil traffic through the key Strait of Hormuz has plunged, and Iran has refused to reopen the waterway.

“Everything points to the Iran War and the Strait of Hormuz,” said Tom Seng, a professor of energy finance at Texas Christian University.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright offered few specifics on when the nation’s drivers might see relief at the gas pump, acknowledging that prices are higher now than Labor Day 2025.

“Yes, they’re higher today, but we’re doing everything we can to push them down,” Wright said Sunday on ABC’s “This Week.”

The national average for regular gas prices is still well below the record of $5.02 a gallon set in June 2022.

But diesel is a different story: It hit a national average of $5.85 a gallon Friday, a record.

Trucks and other freight delivery systems use a lot of diesel, and that increased transportation cost is being passed on to consumers, whether at the grocery store or through package delivery services.

“It doesn’t really seem like there’s an end to it,” Collins said.

Gas prices typically drop as the summer driving season ends and refineries turn to making a cheaper winter blend.

But Seng said there are other factors this year even beyond the volatile situation in the Middle East that make future prices unpredictable. U.S. refineries are working at 98% capacity, many in the unusually harsh Texas heat. If there are problems there or a hurricane knocks some systems offline, prices will struggle to drop.

And it’s not just a Middle East problem. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian refineries are squeezing diesel supplies. Chinese refiners are seeing declining outputs as well, said Matthew Metzgar, a clinical professor of economics at UNC Charlotte.

“There’s just less gasoline coming out of those refineries,” Metzgar said.

Wright, the energy secretary, said the Trump administration was taking steps to increase production and that the markets forecast lower prices in the coming months.

“If you look at the futures prices, if you wanted to buy today in bulk gasoline for two months out in November, it’s about $0.35 cheaper than it is today. So the marketplace thinks gasoline prices are going to move meaningfully lower,” he said.

Geopolitically, though, there is little a driver can do to knock down gas prices.

But using price apps can help save a little money, especially on long trips where gas by the interstate could be 10 to 15 cents per gallon more expensive than at stations a short drive down the road, Metzgar said.

—Jeffrey Collins, Associated Press

Associated Press videojournalist Mingson Lau and reporter Gary Fields contributed.

item.title: Ultra-rich ‘super billionaires’ have quadrupled their share of global wealth over the last decade
item.description:
The planet has more billionaires than ever before. According to a new report, the total wealth of the super-rich is growing, but that doesn’t mean wealth is being spread evenly across the population—or across generations for that matter.

In fact, a large percentage of billionaires are well into their golden years.

The data comes from the 2026 Billionaire Census Report, conducted by the global wealth intelligence company Altrada.

Most billionaires fall into the relatively lower categories of wealth. People in the $1-2 billion category or the $2-5 billion category make up a large majority of the billionaire class at 82%, according to the report.

However, the number of those at the very top who have achieved “super billionaire” status is growing.

Globally, there are 29 super billionaires who each have more than $50 billion.

“Members of this elite tier have recorded by far the most dynamic wealth generation over the past decade, underlining the hyper-concentration of global wealth at the very top,” the report explains.

The group makes up only 0.7% of the billionaire population, but it holds 27% of all billionaire wealth, a number that rose by 16.3% in two years.

Back in 2017, there were only 10 super billionaires.

More people joining the billionaires club

In 2025, the number of billionaires in the world rose by 8.2%, for an addition of 287 individuals who achieved billionaire-level wealth, largely a result of AI investments.

The world now has 3,795 billionaires, an all-time high, the report says.

Still, while there are more billionaires and more super billionaires than ever, that doesn’t mean that the world is getting wealthier.

Most of the wealth is held by U.S. billionaires, where 1,265 individuals have $6,688 billion. The United States is trailed by China, which has $1,438 billion spread over 363 billionaires. Germany came in third with 221 billionaires who have $806 billion.

Most of the super wealthy are not famous pop stars or young influencers who have managed to slay the algorithm. They are filthy-rich men of a certain age.

The average age of billionaires is 71, according to the report. And almost half of all billionaires are over the age of 70. Only around 9% are 50 and under, Altrada reveals.

Gender imbalance

Unsurprisingly, billionaires are mostly male, as women make up just 13% of the billionaire class.

And, while 62% of billionaires are self-made, a large portion of them didn’t earn their wealth whatsoever, or didn’t earn it without a hefty inheritance that set them up for success.

Overall, nearly 40% of the world’s wealthiest individuals achieved billionaire status, at least in part, due to inheritance.

While the over 70s are hoarding the world’s wealth, given that they can’t live forever (unless anti-aging technology advances more quickly), that will begin to shift in the years ahead.

When it does, younger generations stand to inherit a very pretty penny. Globally, a total of $6.6 trillion is expected to be handed over in the next decade. In North America alone, billionaires are expected to transfer $3.3 trillion by 2035.

item.title: Historically strong 2026 Super El Niño could have this devastating effect on California
item.description:
A lot has been written about how this year’s Super El Niño is likely to be the strongest on record and could result in extreme weather through 2027. But we’re just learning now that it may cause serious damage to California’s coast, impacting sea levels and possibly triggering floods.

El Niño is forecast to raise sea levels along the California coast by about a foot by the middle of next month, according to oceanographer Dillon Amaya at North Carolina State University, CNN reported. That’s because the climate pattern will push water from Mexico and Central America north up to the U.S. coastline.

That may in turn trigger “Kelvin waves”—which unlike typical waves, “slosh up and down, like water in a bathtub,” where they are, in effect, stuck, according to CNN.

“Typically, we think of El Niño and its impact on precipitation, but some of the first indications that El Niño is really occurring are the arrival of these coastally trapped waves,” Amaya told CNN.

At the same time that El Niño is expected to produce those waves and higher sea levels, California is also expecting regularly occurring king tides, or “astronomically high tides,” climate scientist Daniel Swain at the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources told American Community Media.

As a result, Swain said there is an elevated risk of coastal erosion and severe flooding around the San Francisico Bay Area, for low-lying towns and communities sitting 6 feet or less above sea level.

“El Niño doesn’t guarantee a wet winter in California,” he said. “But a very strong, potentially historically strong event, which is our expectation for this year, likely increases the amount of precipitation that California will experience this winter.”

item.title: Lawmakers reach for AI legislation after researchers warn of extinction
item.description:
Welcome to AI Decoded, Fast Company‘s weekly newsletter that breaks down the most important news in the world of AI. I’m Mark Sullivan, a senior writer at Fast Company, covering emerging tech, AI, and tech policy.

Sign up to receive this newsletter every week via email here. And if you have comments on this issue and/or ideas for future ones, drop me a line at sullivan@fastcompany.com, and follow me on X @thesullivan.

“It’s time to sound the alarm”

The resignation of the Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon, and his statements afterward, have sent shock waves through the AI community. Coxon, who left the company on Tuesday, tweeted that he spent the last three years working on model pretraining research at both Anthropic and OpenAI, and that the people building the models “earnestly believe it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” “They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives,” Coxon wrote. His post has been viewed more than 70 million times. The resignation follows incidents in which artificial intelligence agents broke out of their sandboxes, accessed the internet, and broke into other companies’ servers.

Now the shock waves have moved into political circles; a number of high-profile figures are calling for an immediate halt to frontier model research.

The Illinois governor, JB Pritzker, a Democrat, referenced Coxon’s resignation and called for industry and federal action:

“It’s time to sound the alarm – louder – on reining in Artificial Intelligence. It’s becoming more clear the threat AI poses to humanity, so I’m calling for immediate action from the industry and Washington.”

In a follow-up post, Pritzker called for an end to big tech lobbying against safety rules and for congressional hearings on AI development. “When AI researchers are whistleblowing, we need to listen,” he wrote. “They are telling us this technology could be as dangerous as a nuclear bomb.”

Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for a U.S. Senate seat in Michigan, quoted the same Coxon thread:

“Most tech geeks don’t resign from their roles because . . . the tech they’re building could end humanity. How we change the incentives leading AI labs down this path and protect against these existential risks are defining political questions of our time.”

Later the same day, he posted a video: “AI development is moving faster than our ability to assure its safety. It’s time to hit pause until we can assure it won’t . . . destroy us.”

Chris Van Hollen, U.S. senator from Maryland and also a Democrat, quoted Coxon and called both for slowing AI research and for new regulations:

“Anyone still denying the risks posed by unregulated AI should read this thread. It’s time to pump the brakes & take action NOW. We need: Mandatory safeguards; A comprehensive testing regime; Urgent dialogue with China, before & during President Xi’s visit to DC this month.”

U.S. Representative Pat Ryan, a New York Democrat, called for better “pacing” of AI research:

“1) We need emergency hearings on pacing the frontier – NOW!! 2) This November, we need to elect leaders willing to stand up to AI oligarchs and fight for the American people.”

After news that OpenAI agents had broken into Hugging Face servers, Ryan tweeted:

“When I wrote a letter with [Texas Democratic representative Greg Casar] to OpenAI last month (post Hugging Face), we asked whether other similar incidents had occurred. They refused to tell us. Then this comes out. The House Democratic Majority arrives in January. I look forward to the public hearings.”

Evan Hubinger, alignment science team lead at Anthropic, tweeted in support of Coxon’s views. “I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to,” he wrote.

Samuel Marks, who runs Anthropic’s scalable oversight division, wrote in a personal capacity that developers continue building despite the risk of human extinction because of commercial incentives and a belief that they are racing less responsible competitors, Variety reported.

Bernie Sanders, the independent U.S. senator from Vermont, wrote Wednesday that “Mr. Coxon is right” and said he will introduce legislation to ban superintelligence and pause AI development, Forbes reported. The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act would halt development of AI systems capable of surpassing human intelligence and impose a temporary pause on other advanced systems until a new federal regulator sets safety rules.

U.S. representatives Greg Casar, a Texas Democrat; Lori Trahan, a Massachusetts Democrat; and Anna Paulina Luna, a Florida Republican, along with Governor Ron DeSantis of Florida, a Republican, and the former presidential candidate Andrew Yang have also responded to Coxon’s resignation, sounding the alarm about out-of-control AI development.

The Trump administration, meanwhile, has generally pushed to accelerate AI development while reducing what it considers burdensome regulation.

U.S. agencies accuse 6 Chinese AI companies of industrial-scale model copying

The National Security Agency, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, and the FBI issued a joint advisory Tuesday accusing Chinese AI companies of extracting the proprietary functionalities and capabilities of American frontier models, Engadget reported. The advisory names DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Alibaba, MiniMax, StepFun, and Z.AI, and says they took billions of tokens across millions of exchanges from Anthropic’s Claude, OpenAI’s GPT, Google’s Gemini, and xAI’s Grok since at least late 2024. The agencies said the practice is tacitly encouraged but not directed by political leaders in Beijing, and that distillation is the critical core of these firms’ development rather than a supplement.

OpenAI says 10,000 agents solved a Millennium Prize problem

OpenAI published a proposed solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of seven Millennium Prize Problems set by the Clay Mathematics Institute, each carrying a $1 million award. OpenAI says roughly 10,000 agents running on an unreleased internal model reached the result on September 5, about 88 hours after the first agents launched, exchanging 2.7 million messages and generating about 130 billion output tokens. Checking and formalizing the proof took another 17 hours using GPT-6 Astra.

Suno launches models trained on licensed music

Suno released a new generation of music models that it developed with Warner Music Group, BMG, and Believe, Jack Brody, Suno’s chief product officer, told Axios. They’re the first models Suno has built under its music industry partnerships, and the company still blocks users from prompting it to make a song in the likeness of a known artist or song. Reportedly, Suno will retire its previous models, a portion of revenue will be shared with the partners from launch day, and rights holders are responsible for distributing that money. 

Mistral raises 3 billion euros, Europe’s largest private tech round

The European AI lab Mistral AI raised 3 billion euros (almost $3.5 billion) at a post-money valuation above 21 billion euros, which the company describes as the largest equity fundraising round ever completed by a European technology company. Samsung Electronics led the round with Scaleup Europe Fund and an existing investor, PSG Equity. TechCrunch reported that new backers include Advent and BlackRock, that existing backers a16z, Nvidia, and Salesforce Ventures participated, and that the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg joined as a new investor. Mistral says it will use the money to expand frontier research, scale compute capacity for training, and grow internationally.

Google will spend 13 billion euros on Finnish data centers

Google said Wednesday it will invest at least 13 billion euros ($15.1 billion) in AI infrastructure in Finland, its largest single investment in Europe, CNBC reported. Bloomberg reported the money will go toward at least three new data centers plus an expansion of the company’s existing site in Hamina over the next two years. In its own announcement, Google says the investment includes clean energy projects and community funds.
